note: The Inferno, the first of the poem's three parts. Dante names his own canto and book here, in an unusually plain opening.
The fourth ditch of Malebolge, seen from the top of the bridge. It holds the soothsayers: seers, astrologers and magicians who claimed to read the future.
Church processions in which the people walk slowly behind the clergy, chanting prayers. These souls walk at the same pace, but in silence.
The punishment fits the sin exactly, as Virgil says below. They tried to see ahead into the future, which belongs to God alone, so their heads are twisted round and they can only look behind them.
One of about twenty places where Dante turns and speaks to the reader. He asks to be excused for weeping.
The human body was made in God's image. What moves Dante is not the pain of the damned but the sight of that image wrenched out of shape.
Virgil's harshest rebuke in the poem. Dante wept for Francesca in Inferno 5 and for others since, and was not scolded. This far down, pity for the damned is no longer allowed.

quote: Here pity lives only when it is dead
note: A famous line built on one word. The Italian pietà means both pity and piety. In Hell, piety, a right love of God's justice, lives only when pity for the damned is dead.
A disputed line in the Italian. It may mean someone who pities those God has judged, or someone who tries to bend God's judgment to his own will, as the soothsayers did.

context: The first three seers Virgil points out all come from Latin poems about ancient wars, two of them about Thebes.

note: A seer, and one of the seven kings who attacked Thebes. He foresaw that he would die in the war and tried to stay out of it. In the battle the earth opened and swallowed him, chariot and all. The story is told in the Thebaid of the Roman poet Statius.

quote: made his shoulders into a chest
note: His head faces backward, so what was his back is now in front of his face.

context: Virgil tells only the story of his changes of sex, from Ovid's Metamorphoses. The seer's body was twisted out of its nature in life, as it is twisted now.

note: In Ovid, Tiresias struck two mating snakes with his staff and was turned into a woman. Seven years later he found the same snakes, struck them again and became a man.
An Etruscan soothsayer in Lucan's poem on the Roman civil war, the Pharsalia. He reads the entrails of a sacrificed bull and foretells the war between Caesar and Pompey.
The mountains above the ancient town of Luni, on the coast of northwest Tuscany. The white marble of Carrara is still quarried there.

context: Virgil turns from her to a long account of how his own city was founded. In Purgatorio 22 a "daughter of Tiresias" is listed among the souls in Limbo, a contradiction that has never been explained.

note: Virgil was born near Mantua, as he told Dante when they met in Inferno 1.

quote: Let me tell you her story
note: The digression has a purpose. In the Middle Ages Virgil himself had a reputation as a magician and a prophet. Many readers think Dante has him tell this story to clear his name, and his city's, of any link with sorcery.
Tiresias, the seer just pointed out.
Thebes, where the god Bacchus was born. After the war of the seven kings the city fell under the tyrant Creon.
The old Latin name of Lake Garda, the largest lake in Italy, at the foot of the Alps between Verona and Brescia.
The Alpine county north of the lake, named after its lords' castle near Merano.

Garda is a town on the lake's eastern shore, and Val Camonica a long valley to the west. The mountains between them drain into the lake. Dante's word for them in the next line is "Pennino", and its reading and meaning are disputed in the Italian text.

quote: At the center sits a place
note: A spot on the lake where three dioceses met, so that each of the three bishops would be standing in his own territory and could give a blessing there. Which spot Dante means is uncertain.
A fortress town at the southern end of the lake, where the river Mincio flows out. In Dante's time it belonged to the lords of Verona and guarded their border against Brescia and Bergamo.
Virgil's native river, which he praises in his own poems. It runs from Lake Garda past Mantua to the Po.
Now Governolo, a village southeast of Mantua where the Mincio enters the Po, the great river of northern Italy.
Manto. The Italian word can mean cruel or wild. In the Aeneid she is no virgin: she has a son. Dante's Virgil changes the story.

context: In this account the city takes only its name and its site from the sorceress. It was built after her death by ordinary people who wanted the safety of the marsh.

note: Ancient cities were named after casting lots or taking omens. Mantua's founders used no such arts. The point is that the city has nothing to do with divination.

Alberto da Casalodi, a count who ruled Mantua. Pinamonte dei Bonacolsi advised him to win over the people by sending the leading nobles into exile. With Casalodi's supporters gone, Pinamonte seized the city in 1272 and killed or drove out many of the remaining families.
The different version is Virgil's own. In the Aeneid (Book 10), Mantua is founded by Ocnus, the son of Manto, who names it after his mother. Dante makes Virgil correct his own poem.

quote: when Greece was emptied of men
note: The Trojan War. Every Greek man of fighting age had sailed for Troy.
The chief seer of the Greek army at Troy.
The Greek port where the fleet gathered to sail for Troy. The seers chose the favorable moment to cut the mooring ropes and set out.

In Book 2 of the Aeneid he is a Greek sent to ask Apollo's oracle when the fleet should sail home. Virgil's poem doesn't call him an augur or place him at Aulis: Dante's memory of the passage, or his reading of it, differs from the text.
The Aeneid. In medieval terms a tragedy was a poem in the high style. Dante calls his own poem a comedy, in a humbler style and with a happy ending, at the start of the next canto and in Inferno 16.
Dante's proud claim, put in Virgil's mouth, that he knows the Aeneid from beginning to end.

Michael Scot, a Scottish scholar who died about 1235. He translated Aristotle and Arabic science into Latin at Toledo and served as astrologer at the court of the emperor Frederick II. Legend soon made him a wizard.

The best-known astrologer of thirteenth-century Italy, from Forlì, and the author of a large textbook of astrology. He advised lords on when to give battle, among them Guido da Montefeltro, whom Dante meets in Inferno 27.
"Toothless", the nickname of a shoemaker of Parma who won fame as a prophet in the later thirteenth century. Dante mentions him with scorn in another work, the Convivio.
Potions, and figures made in a victim's likeness to be pierced or melted. These are village witches, nameless beside the famous seers.
The moon. Where we see a man in the moon, Italian folklore saw Cain carrying a bundle of thorns, banished there for killing Abel.

Seville stands for the western edge of the known world. The moon is setting in the west, on the line between the hemisphere of land and the hemisphere of ocean. A full moon sets as the sun rises, so it is about six in the morning of Holy Saturday.
The night Dante was lost in the dark forest, the moon was full and helped him. Inferno 1 says nothing of moonlight: this is a detail added afterward.
